stages.name: Gathering
stages.crowd: Socializing, testing the vibe, minds still open.
stages.floor: Anticipation. The room is arriving, not performing.
stages.frequency: Favor warmth in the low mids. Keep sub and presence in the background so the door still feels like a door.
stages.mix: Long intros and clean grids. Same-key or relative-key moves. Do not slam a peak record into an empty floor.
paragraphs: The Gathering is the open. You are not chasing a reaction yet. You are telling the room what kind of night this is, and giving people permission to step closer to the booth.
Program length. Intros can run 32 to 64 bars. A first drop should feel like a hello, not a headline. Development after that drop is where regulars decide if they trust you.
If a record is loud but has no intro and no air, it is not an opener, no matter how good the tune is. Save it.
play: Warm low-mids, moderate groove, readable drums
Intros long enough to talk over and still land the one
Minor or major is fine if the energy stays low
avoid: Full-tilt kicks and smashed masters from the first record
Vocal anthems that spend the hook too early
Key clashes while the floor is still sparse

stages.name: Confidence
stages.crowd: Starting to move. Trust is building. Eyes come up to the booth.
stages.floor: Momentum. Bodies commit, conversations get shorter.
stages.frequency: Low-mids still carry the body. Bass weight can rise, but presence should not shred yet.
stages.mix: Step the energy up without breaking the key path. Neighboring Camelot numbers, same letter, are the clean lift.
paragraphs: Confidence is the hour where the night stops being background music. The job is trust: a steady grid, a groove people can find, and a lift they feel before they can name it.
Builds are short. The first drop has to pay off the promise of the Gathering without spending the biggest record in the bag. A second drop, longer than the first, is where the floor locks to you.
If the room is still talking through the hook, you are early, not failing. Raise density and bass weight. Do not jump to Chaos to prove a point.
play: Even drums and a groove that survives a 16-bar blend
Warm records with a clear one and a usable outro
Energy in the middle of your library, not the top
avoid: Fake-outs and switch-ups the floor has not earned
Dark, dry rollers that make the room feel closed
Doubling the tempo jump and the key jump in one mix

stages.name: Peak Hype
stages.crowd: Hands up. The scream is the downbeat. This is the memory.
stages.floor: Explosion. Density, hooks, and a drop that the whole room can point at.
stages.frequency: Bass weight at 60–120 Hz and presence at 2–5 kHz. This is impact and vocal cut, not sub hypnosis.
stages.mix: You can tighten blends. Outros get shorter. Keep one harmonic thread so the peak feels like a run, not a playlist.
paragraphs: The fake drop matters. Take the floor to the edge, deny them once, then pay them. A VIP or second drop is the souvenir. The outro should be quick — you are already holding the next anthem.
A record can be famous and still be wrong here if it has no lift. Peak is a shape: rising tension, a hit, almost no recovery inside the record itself.
play: High loudness, heavy bass weight, a hook or chant
One clear peak, not three competing ones
Tension that resolves on the drop, not before it
avoid: Long hypnotic rollers with no event
Soft warm-up tools dressed up by a loud master
Back-to-back key clashes just because both tunes are big

stages.name: Chaos
stages.crowd: Adrenaline, surprise, raw emotion. They want to be shocked, not soothed.
stages.floor: Controlled madness. The grid can lurch. The DJ still knows where the one is.
stages.frequency: Presence and bass weight stay high. Flux and hard onsets matter more than a pretty low-mid.
stages.mix: Shorter blends, switch-ups, and fake-outs. Harmonic rules loosen, but a total clash on every handoff just sounds lost.
paragraphs: Chaos is the spike after the anthem, not a second copy of Peak Hype. Peak is the memory. Chaos is the jolt that keeps that memory from flattening into a playlist.
Program switches: drop, flip the drum pattern, drop again, fake a landing, drop a third time. The floor should laugh or yell. If they only look confused, you left the one behind.
Keep it short. An hour of adrenaline is a set. Two hours is a headache. Sketch Hours and Locked In are how you survive what you just did.
play: Hard onsets, bright attack, unstable energy inside the record
Switch-ups that still have a countable bar
Records that feel slightly too much, on purpose
avoid: Smooth warm rollers and long emotional breakdowns
Another singalong with the same kick as the peak
Effects with no drum underneath

stages.name: Locked In
stages.crowd: Flow state. Nobody is thinking. They are just moving.
stages.floor: Hypnotic. Time gets unreliable. The kick is the room.
stages.frequency: Sub from 20–60 Hz is the foundation. Presence and vocals step back so the pattern can loop without fatigue.
stages.mix: This is the long blend hour. One possible harmonic route is 8A to 8B to 9B to 10B: A minor, C, G, D. Same-number major/minor flip, then adjacent numbers on the same letter. These moves do not guarantee an energy rise.
paragraphs: Locked In is where a good DJ disappears. The record does not need a hook. It needs a pattern that can be varied for minutes without the floor noticing the seam.
Think in loops, not songs. A variation every 16 bars is enough: a hat opens, a sub note moves, an effect breathes and leaves. Minimal breaks. If you pull the kick out, earn the return.
play: Even kick, high self-similarity, low vocal
Sub that you feel more than you hear on a phone
Intros and outros long enough for a 32-bar blend
avoid: Anthem vocals and drop-chasing
Wild tempo swings inside a hypnotic run
Bright airy tops that pull the room out of the pocket

stages.name: Sketch Hours
stages.crowd: Deep immersion. Time distortion. Survivors only.
stages.floor: Underground. Dark, minimal, a private agreement with whoever stayed.
stages.frequency: Sub and dryness. Air and low-mid warmth are the wrong paint. If it sounds expensive and wide, it is probably a Sunrise record.
stages.mix: Stay in a narrow harmonic lane. Rollers can run long. A vocal, even a pretty one, wakes people up.
paragraphs: Sketch Hours is not ‘late and still loud.’ It is the room after the tourists leave. Dark, minimal, almost no voice, a roller that could run another five minutes and nobody would complain.
Open with atmosphere, bring drums in late, then live in the roller. Evolution is a filter or a ghost note, not a new chorus. The outro can be long because the next record should arrive like weather.
Darkness here is not a sad lyric. It is low air, low presence, and usually a minor color. A bright hat pattern can fake a high centroid and still be a roller. Trust the low end and the repetition.
play: Dry subs, small kits, almost no vocal
Low loudness wobble across several minutes
Minor keys and a narrow Camelot neighborhood
avoid: Hands-up hooks and festival supersaws
Big breakdowns that reset the spell
Warm, wide, major-key ‘after’ records — those are Rebirth or Sunrise

stages.name: Rebirth
stages.crowd: Emotional release. Connection. Smiles come back.
stages.floor: Uplift. Warmth returns without pretending it is midnight again.
stages.frequency: Low-mids for body and air above 10 kHz for space. Presence can return if it is musical, not abrasive.
stages.mix: Let a breakdown breathe. Coming out of Sketch, one relative-major move (A to B on the same number) feels like sunrise indoors.
paragraphs: Rebirth is the thaw. The dark hour did its job. Now chords, voice, and a real release remind the room that other people are still here.
Give the melodic intro time. A piano or vocal break is the point, not a mistake in the energy curve. The big drop after that break should feel like relief, not like another peak-time weapon.

Emotion in this system is shape: dynamics, a real dip, and body in the low mids. It is not a sadness score and it is not a streaming mood tag. If the record is flat and smashed, it will not carry this hour.
play: Warm chords, a breakdown you can stand inside
Voice used as a human signal, not a hype chant
Air and space after a long stretch of dry sub
avoid: Another distorted switch-up
Dropping straight back to Peak Hype volume
Cold, vocal-less rollers that refuse to open

stages.name: Sunrise
stages.floor: Closure. The night exhales. Silence is an instrument.
stages.frequency: Air and softness. Energy and aggression should be near the bottom of the library. Sub can remain, but it should bloom, not punch.
stages.mix: Slow the handoffs. An outro can dissolve instead of ending on a hot cue. Leave a bar of room tone if the system will allow it.
paragraphs: Ambient intro, a simple groove, one gentle drop, then atmosphere that is allowed to thin out. The last move can be smaller than the one before it. That is the point.
Recovery is how well a record lets the room reset: a breakdown, air, and less loudness than what just happened. Play it after the night, not instead of the night.
play: Spacious tops, low aggression, a fading grid
Major color or a very gentle minor
Records you could end on, including near-silence
avoid: One more peak ‘for the stragglers’
Dark warehouse rollers that reopen Sketch Hours
Hard cuts into the next tune with no landing

dimensions.name: Darkness
dimensions.text: Low air, low presence, and usually a minor key. A bright hat pattern is not automatically ‘happy.’

dimensions.name: Warmth
dimensions.text: Body in the low mids, roughly 120–500 Hz. This is Confidence and Rebirth, not sub-bass punch.

dimensions.name: Groove
dimensions.text: How even the drum grid is. A record can groove without being a roller.

dimensions.name: Aggression
dimensions.text: Onsets, spectral flux, and a smashed crest. Presence bite belongs to Peak and Chaos.

dimensions.name: Emotion
dimensions.text: Shape and depth: dynamics, a real release, and low-mid body. Not a streaming mood label.

dimensions.name: Vocal presence
dimensions.text: Energy in the voice band. Leads and pads can score here too, so use your ears on instrumental hooks.

dimensions.name: Energy
dimensions.text: Loudness plus bass weight plus how often the record attacks. Raw peak volume is not the night arc.

dimensions.name: Tension
dimensions.text: A rise into the loudest part of the record. Chaos lives here. Gathering should not.

dimensions.name: Release
dimensions.text: The size of the biggest drop in energy inside the record — the breakdown that lets people breathe.

dimensions.name: Roller index
dimensions.text: Steady loudness, a pattern that resembles itself one bar later, low vocal, low flux.

dimensions.name: Recovery
dimensions.text: Space, air, and less loudness than the record before it. This is how you reset a room.

dimensions.name: Transition
dimensions.text: Long intro, long outro, stable grid. Real compatibility is still the next tune’s key and tempo.
